claim: Xanthohumol (XN) and tetrahydroxanthohumol (TXN) attenuate high-fat diet-induced obesity and metabolic syndrome in C57Bl/6J mice.
source: We previously reported xanthohumol (XN), and its synthetic derivative tetrahydro-XN (TXN), attenuates high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity and metabolic syndrome in C57Bl/6J mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: TXN reduced weight gain in mice fed a 60% high-fat diet.
source: Non-supplemented mice were unable to adapt their caloric intake to 60% HFD, resulting in obesity and hepatic steatosis; however, TXN reduced weight gain and decreased hepatic steatosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mouse feeding study described in the manuscript.

claim: TXN decreased hepatic steatosis in mice fed a high-fat diet.
source: Non-supplemented mice were unable to adapt their caloric intake to 60% HFD, resulting in obesity and hepatic steatosis; however, TXN reduced weight gain and decreased hepatic steatosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mouse feeding study.

claim: Liver transcriptomics indicated that TXN might antagonize lipogenic PPARγ actions in vivo.
source: Liver transcriptomics indicated that TXN might antagonize lipogenic PPARγ actions in vivo.
evidence: This claim is based on RNA-seq data analysis from liver tissue.

claim: XN and TXN inhibited rosiglitazone-induced 3T3-L1 cell differentiation.
source: XN and TXN inhibited rosiglitazone-induced 3T3-L1 cell differentiation concomitant with decreased expression of lipogenesis-related genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell culture experiments with 3T3-L1 cells.

claim: XN and TXN decreased expression of lipogenesis-related genes in 3T3-L1 cells.
source: XN and TXN inhibited rosiglitazone-induced 3T3-L1 cell differentiation concomitant with decreased expression of lipogenesis-related genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data from cell culture experiments.

claim: XN and TXN bind to PPARγ with an IC50 similar to pioglitazone.
source: A peroxisome proliferator activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) competitive binding assay showed that XN and TXN bind to PPARγ with an IC50 similar to pioglitazone and 8–10 times stronger than oleate.
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive binding assay data.

claim: XN and TXN bind to PPARγ 8-10 times stronger than oleate.
source: A peroxisome proliferator activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) competitive binding assay showed that XN and TXN bind to PPARγ with an IC50 similar to pioglitazone and 8–10 times stronger than oleate.
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive binding assay data comparing IC50 values.

claim: Molecular docking simulations demonstrated that XN and TXN bind in the PPARγ ligand-binding domain pocket.
source: Molecular docking simulations demonstrated that XN and TXN bind in the PPARγ ligand-binding domain pocket.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational molecular docking studies.

claim: XN and TXN act as antagonists of PPARγ.
source: Our findings are consistent with XN and TXN acting as antagonists of PPARγ.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple lines of experimental evidence including binding assays, cell culture, and in vivo studies.

claim: About one-quarter of the US population suffers from NAFLD.
source: About one-quarter of the US population suffers from NAFLD (Estes et al., 2018), with rates in the rest of the world ranging from 14% in Africa to 32% in the Middle East (Younossi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published epidemiological data.

claim: NAFLD rates in the rest of the world range from 14% in Africa to 32% in the Middle East.
source: About one-quarter of the US population suffers from NAFLD (Estes et al., 2018), with rates in the rest of the world ranging from 14% in Africa to 32% in the Middle East (Younossi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published epidemiological data.

claim: No FDA-approved drugs exist for the treatment of NAFLD.
source: Unfortunately, no FDA-approved drugs exist for its treatment.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the current state of NAFLD treatment options.

claim: Sustained healthy lifestyle changes and weight loss are the only interventions proven effective in preventing the onset and progression of NAFLD.
source: Sustained healthy lifestyle changes and weight loss are the only interventions proven effective in preventing the onset and progression of NAFLD (Stefan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published clinical evidence.

claim: PPARγ is important in hepatic lipogenesis.
source: Given that peroxisome proliferator activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) is important in hepatic lipogenesis (Sharma and Staels, 2007), it has attracted considerable attention as a therapeutic target for NAFLD (Almeda-Valdés et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research on PPARγ function.

claim: PPARγ has attracted considerable attention as a therapeutic target for NAFLD.
source: Given that peroxisome proliferator activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) is important in hepatic lipogenesis (Sharma and Staels, 2007), it has attracted considerable attention as a therapeutic target for NAFLD (Almeda-Valdés et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on NAFLD therapeutics.

claim: Attenuated PPARγ activity in heterozygous Pparg-deficient mice protects against high-fat diet-induced obesity, liver steatosis, and adipocyte hypertrophy.
source: Attenuated PPARγ activity in heterozygous Pparg-deficient (Pparg+/−) C57Bl/6J mice protects against high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity, liver steatosis, and adipocyte hypertrophy; however, treatment with the PPARγ agonist pioglitazone (PGZ) abrogates the protection against adipocyte hypertrophy (enlarged adipocytes) and decreases insulin sensitivity (Kubota et al., 1999), suggesting a potential beneficial use for PPARγ antagonists to treat hepatic steatosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published mouse genetic studies.

claim: Treatment with pioglitazone abrogates the protection against adipocyte hypertrophy in Pparg+/- mice and decreases insulin sensitivity.
source: Attenuated PPARγ activity in heterozygous Pparg-deficient (Pparg+/−) C57Bl/6J mice protects against high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity, liver steatosis, and adipocyte hypertrophy; however, treatment with the PPARγ agonist pioglitazone (PGZ) abrogates the protection against adipocyte hypertrophy (enlarged adipocytes) and decreases insulin sensitivity (Kubota et al., 1999), suggesting a potential beneficial use for PPARγ antagonists to treat hepatic steatosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published experimental data.

claim: PPARγ antagonists tanshinone IIA, β-cryptoxanthine, protopanaxatriol, isorhamnetin, and Gleevec improved multiple metabolic parameters in diet-induced obese mice.
source: PPARγ antagonists tanshinone IIA (Gong et al., 2009), β-cryptoxanthine (Goto et al., 2013), protopanaxatriol (Zhang et al., 2014), isorhamnetin (Zhang et al., 2016), and Gleevec (Choi et al., 2016) improved multiple metabolic parameters in diet-induced obese (DIO) mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies on PPARγ antagonists.

claim: Moderate inhibition of PPARγ activity may reduce the risk for developing hepatic steatosis induced by diet.
source: These observations strongly suggest that moderate inhibition of PPARγ activity may reduce the risk for developing hepatic steatosis induced by diet, and PPARγ antagonists may be useful for the treatment and prevention of NAFLD.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cited studies on PPARγ antagonists.

claim: PPARγ antagonists may be useful for the treatment and prevention of NAFLD.
source: These observations strongly suggest that moderate inhibition of PPARγ activity may reduce the risk for developing hepatic steatosis induced by diet, and PPARγ antagonists may be useful for the treatment and prevention of NAFLD.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on inference from cited studies.

claim: Xanthohumol is a prenylated flavonoid found in hops (Humulus lupulus L.).
source: Xanthohumol (XN), a prenylated flavonoid found in hops (Humulus lupulus L.), improves multiple parameters of MetS in rat and mouse models (Legette et al., 2014; Miranda et al., 2016; Miranda et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the chemical composition of hops.

claim: Xanthohumol improves multiple parameters of metabolic syndrome in rat and mouse models.
source: Xanthohumol (XN), a prenylated flavonoid found in hops (Humulus lupulus L.), improves multiple parameters of MetS in rat and mouse models (Legette et al., 2014; Miranda et al., 2016; Miranda et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published animal studies.

claim: Tetrahydroxanthohumol is a non-estrogenic synthetic XN derivative.
source: Tetrahydroxanthohumol (TXN), a non-estrogenic synthetic XN derivative (Figure 1), appears more effective in ameliorating MetS in DIO mice than XN possibly due to its 5-, 10-, and 12-fold higher levels in the muscle, plasma, and liver, respectively, as compared with XN (Miranda et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and reference to Figure 1 showing the chemical structure.

claim: TXN appears more effective in ameliorating metabolic syndrome in diet-induced obese mice than XN.
source: Tetrahydroxanthohumol (TXN), a non-estrogenic synthetic XN derivative (Figure 1), appears more effective in ameliorating MetS in DIO mice than XN possibly due to its 5-, 10-, and 12-fold higher levels in the muscle, plasma, and liver, respectively, as compared with XN (Miranda et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published comparative studies.

claim: TXN has 5-, 10-, and 12-fold higher levels in the muscle, plasma, and liver, respectively, compared with XN.
source: Tetrahydroxanthohumol (TXN), a non-estrogenic synthetic XN derivative (Figure 1), appears more effective in ameliorating MetS in DIO mice than XN possibly due to its 5-, 10-, and 12-fold higher levels in the muscle, plasma, and liver, respectively, as compared with XN (Miranda et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published pharmacokinetic data.

claim: XN inhibits differentiation of preadipocytes and induces apoptosis in mature adipocytes.
source: XN inhibits differentiation of preadipocytes and induces apoptosis in mature adipocytes (Yang et al., 2007; Rayalam et al., 2009), attenuates the function of SREBP-1 by repressing its maturation (Miyata et al., 2015) and induces beiging of white adipose tissue (WAT), decreases adipogenesis, and induces lipolysis (Samuels et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published cell culture studies.

claim: XN attenuates the function of SREBP-1 by repressing its maturation.
source: XN inhibits differentiation of preadipocytes and induces apoptosis in mature adipocytes (Yang et al., 2007; Rayalam et al., 2009), attenuates the function of SREBP-1 by repressing its maturation (Miyata et al., 2015) and induces beiging of white adipose tissue (WAT), decreases adipogenesis, and induces lipolysis (Samuels et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published mechanistic studies.

claim: XN induces beiging of white adipose tissue, decreases adipogenesis, and induces lipolysis.
source: XN inhibits differentiation of preadipocytes and induces apoptosis in mature adipocytes (Yang et al., 2007; Rayalam et al., 2009), attenuates the function of SREBP-1 by repressing its maturation (Miyata et al., 2015) and induces beiging of white adipose tissue (WAT), decreases adipogenesis, and induces lipolysis (Samuels et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published studies on adipose tissue biology.

claim: XN and TXN significantly change gut microbiota diversity and abundance, alter bile acid metabolism, and reduce inflammation in mice fed a HFD.
source: We recently showed that XN and TXN significantly change gut microbiota diversity and abundance, alter bile acid metabolism, and reduce inflammation in mice fed a HFD (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous published work.

claim: Supervised machine learning of liver RNA-seq data identified perturbations in PPARγ signaling.
source: Supervised machine learning of liver RNA-seq data identified perturbations in PPARγ signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: XN and TXN act as novel PPARγ antagonists with moderate binding activity.
source: Based on cell culture experiments, a PPARγ competitive binding assay and molecular docking studies, we provide evidence that XN and TXN act as novel PPARγ antagonists with moderate binding activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental approaches including binding assays and computational modeling.

claim: Appropriate functional antagonism of PPARγ is a logical approach to prevent and treat diet-induced liver steatosis and other related metabolic disorders.
source: Collectively, our findings suggest that appropriate functional antagonism of PPARγ is a logical approach to prevent and treat diet-induced liver steatosis and other related metabolic disorders.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings and represents a conclusion.

claim: The structures of XN and TXN could serve as scaffolds for synthesis of more effective compounds to treat NAFLD.
source: The structures of XN and TXN could serve as scaffolds for synthesis of more effective compounds to treat NAFLD.
evidence: This claim is speculative about future drug development possibilities.

claim: C57Bl/6J mice on a 60% HFD gained more body weight than mice on the low-fat diet throughout the experimental period.
source: As expected, C57Bl/6J mice on a 60% HFD (Figure 2A, solid blue line) gained more BW than mice on the low-fat diet (LFD) (Figure 2A, dotted black line) throughout the experimental period (week 1: p<0.05; week 2–16: p<0.001; repeated measures).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TXN supplementation attenuated HFD-induced body weight gain throughout the experimental period.
source: TXN supplementation (Figure 2A, solid dark green line) attenuated HFD-induced BW gain throughout the experimental period (week 1: p<0.05; week 2–16: p<0.001; repeated measures).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 2A with statistical significance.

claim: The higher dosage of XN (HXN), but not the lower dosage (LXN), attenuated HFD-induced BW gain between weeks 8 and 16.
source: XN supplementation showed a dose-response effect: the higher dosage (HXN; Figure 2A, solid red line), but not the lower dosage (LXN; Figure 2A, solid yellow line), attenuated HFD-induced BW gain between weeks 8 and 16.
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight data showing a dose-response relationship.

claim: HFD-fed mice almost doubled their initial body weight, gaining 98.3 ± 2.7%.
source: When BW gain was expressed as % of initial BW, HFD-fed mice almost doubled their initial BW (+98.3 ± 2.7%), whereas TXN-treated mice gained 33% less (+66.2 ± 5.8%, p<0.0001), and LFD-fed mice gained 53% less (+45.8 ± 4.3%, p<0.0001) than HFD-fed mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative body weight gain data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: TXN-treated mice gained 33% less body weight than HFD-fed mice.
source: When BW gain was expressed as % of initial BW, HFD-fed mice almost doubled their initial BW (+98.3 ± 2.7%), whereas TXN-treated mice gained 33% less (+66.2 ± 5.8%, p<0.0001), and LFD-fed mice gained 53% less (+45.8 ± 4.3%, p<0.0001) than HFD-fed mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative body weight gain data with statistical significance.

claim: In male C57Bl/6J mice, a body weight of approximately 40 g is a critical tipping point from which metabolic dysfunction occurs.
source: In male C57Bl/6J mice, a BW of approximately 40 g is a critical tipping point from which metabolic dysfunction occurs (van Beek et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research on mouse metabolic thresholds.

claim: After 16 weeks, mean body weight for mice was LFD (37.5 ± 1.1 g), HFD (50.3 ± 0.6 g), LXN (49.9 ± 1.1 g), HXN (47.4 ± 1.1 g), and TXN (42.2 ± 1.6 g).
source: After 16 weeks, mean BW for these mice was LFD (37.5 ± 1.1 g), HFD (50.3 ± 0.6 g), LXN (49.9 ± 1.1 g), HXN (47.4 ± 1.1 g), and TXN (42.2 ± 1.6 g).
evidence: This claim is supported by direct body weight measurements at study endpoint.

claim: Mice adapted to the HFD by consuming less food than LFD-fed mice over time.
source: Overtime, mice adapted to the HFD by consuming less food than LFD-fed mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by food intake measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The discrepancy in food consumption was insufficient to counteract the elevated caloric intake in HFD-fed mice.
source: However, the discrepancy in food consumption was insufficient to counteract the elevated caloric intake (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of food intake and caloric density data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: HXN-treated mice adapted better to the HFD, indicated by decreased food intake at weeks 1, 6–10, 13, and 16 and decreased caloric intake compared to HFD control mice.
source: HXN-treated mice adapted better to the HFD, indicated by decreased food intake at weeks 1, 6–10, 13, and 16 (p<0.05), and caloric intake (p=0.01) compared to HFD control mice (Figure 2C,D), resulting in less BW gain.
evidence: This claim is supported by food and caloric intake data with statistical significance.

claim: The attenuated body weight gain in TXN-treated mice was not accompanied by a significant reduction in food or caloric intake.
source: In contrast, the attenuated BW gain in TXN-treated mice was not accompanied by a significant reduction in food or caloric intake (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by food and caloric intake data showing no significant difference.

claim: TXN-treated mice showed significantly improved glucose clearance at time points 30 min, 60 min, and 120 min post i.p. injection compared to HFD control mice.
source: Compared to HFD control mice, TXN-treated mice showed significantly improved glucose clearance, as indicated at time points 30 min, 60 min, and 120 min post i.p. injection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, green line; p-values=0.04, 0.02, and <0.01, respectively), as well as a significant lower AUC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, p<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A with statistical significance.

claim: TXN-treated mice had a significantly lower area under the curve in the glucose tolerance test compared to HFD control mice.
source: Compared to HFD control mice, TXN-treated mice showed significantly improved glucose clearance, as indicated at time points 30 min, 60 min, and 120 min post i.p. injection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, green line; p-values=0.04, 0.02, and <0.01, respectively), as well as a significant lower AUC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, p<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by AUC calculations from glucose tolerance test data.

claim: HXN-treated mice showed improved glucose clearance at time points 60 min and 120 min post i.p. injection.
source: HXN-treated mice also showed improved glucose clearance at time points 60 min and 120 min post i.p. injection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, red line; p-values=0.04 and 0.05, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose tolerance test data with statistical significance.

claim: Fasting glycemia was not different between TXN-treated and HFD control mice after 16 weeks of feeding.
source: While fasting glycemia was not different between TXN-treated and HFD control mice after 16 weeks of feeding (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, p=0.56), fasting insulin was significantly improved by TXN treatment as suggested by lower circulating insulin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, p=0.003) and HOMA-IR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, p=0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by fasting glucose measurements showing no significant difference.

claim: Fasting insulin was significantly improved by TXN treatment as indicated by lower circulating insulin and HOMA-IR.
source: While fasting glycemia was not different between TXN-treated and HFD control mice after 16 weeks of feeding (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, p=0.56), fasting insulin was significantly improved by TXN treatment as suggested by lower circulating insulin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, p=0.003) and HOMA-IR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, p=0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by insulin measurements and HOMA-IR calculations with statistical significance.

claim: TXN significantly improved glucose homeostasis.
source: These results indicate that TXN significantly improved glucose homeostasis; XN seems to have a dose response as HXN appears to be more effective than LXN.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from glucose tolerance test and insulin measurements.

claim: XN has a dose response effect on glucose homeostasis, with HXN appearing more effective than LXN.
source: These results indicate that TXN significantly improved glucose homeostasis; XN seems to have a dose response as HXN appears to be more effective than LXN.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of glucose tolerance test results between different XN doses.

claim: HFD mice had greater fat mass than LFD mice.
source: HFD-induced BW gain was primarily body fat accumulation, as indicated by measurements obtained from DEXA scans. HFD mice had greater fat mass than LFD mice (p<0.0001; Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by DEXA scan measurements of body composition.

claim: There is a strong relationship between caloric intake and fat mass among groups (r = +0.52; p<0.0001).
source: Linear regression of total fat mass to total caloric intake revealed a strong relationship between caloric intake and fat mass among groups (r = +0.52; p<0.0001) and within LFD-fed mice (r = +0.79; p=0.002; Figure 3A1).
evidence: This claim is supported by linear regression analysis of fat mass and caloric intake data.

claim: Caloric intake was not correlated to fat mass in any HFD group.
source: In contrast, caloric intake was not correlated to fat mass in any HFD group (Figures 3A, 2-5), indicating a disconnection between caloric intake and fat mass after prolonged HFD consumption.
evidence: This claim is supported by linear regression analysis showing no correlation in HFD groups.

claim: Supplementation with HXN decreased body fat mass by 9.93% on HFD.
source: Supplementation with HXN (−9.93%; p<0.05) and even more so with TXN (−27.7%; p<0.001) decreased body fat mass on HFD (Figure 3A), indicating that HXN and TXN attenuated the HFD-induced body fat accumulation and that this effect was not explained by changes to caloric intake (Figures 3A, 4-5).
evidence: This claim is supported by DEXA scan measurements with statistical significance.

claim: Supplementation with TXN decreased body fat mass by 27.7% on HFD.
source: Supplementation with HXN (−9.93%; p<0.05) and even more so with TXN (−27.7%; p<0.001) decreased body fat mass on HFD (Figure 3A), indicating that HXN and TXN attenuated the HFD-induced body fat accumulation and that this effect was not explained by changes to caloric intake (Figures 3A, 4-5).
evidence: This claim is supported by DEXA scan measurements with statistical significance.

claim: The effect of HXN and TXN on body fat accumulation was not explained by changes to caloric intake.
source: Supplementation with HXN (−9.93%; p<0.05) and even more so with TXN (−27.7%; p<0.001) decreased body fat mass on HFD (Figure 3A), indicating that HXN and TXN attenuated the HFD-induced body fat accumulation and that this effect was not explained by changes to caloric intake (Figures 3A, 4-5).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis showing no correlation between caloric intake and fat mass in treatment groups.

claim: The expandability of eWAT in male mice is an indicator of metabolic health.
source: Prior studies have reported that the expandability of eWAT in male mice is an indicator of metabolic health.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research on adipose tissue biology.

claim: Mouse sWAT and mWAT will continue to expand with body weight, whereas eWAT expansion diminishes after mouse body weight reaches about 40 g.
source: Mouse sWAT and mWAT will continue to expand with BW, whereas eWAT expansion diminishes after mouse BW reaches about 40 g (van Beek et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research on adipose tissue depot-specific expansion.

claim: Supplementation with HXN and TXN mitigated hepatic steatosis, independent of caloric intake.
source: Supplementation with HXN (p<0.05) and TXN (p<0.01) mitigated hepatic steatosis, independent of caloric intake (Figures 3B, 4–5).
evidence: This claim is supported by hepatic lipid area measurements with statistical significance.

claim: Mice consuming HFD had higher energy expenditure than mice on LFD.
source: Mice consuming HFD and mice supplemented with LXN had higher (p<0.05) energy expenditure than mice on LFD, HXN, and TXN (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by indirect calorimetry measurements.

claim: Caloric intake was positively correlated with energy expenditure in LFD-, LXN-, HXN-, and TXN-fed mice but not in HFD mice.
source: Caloric intake was positively correlated with energy expenditure in LFD- (Figure 3C1), LXN- (Figure 3C3), HXN- (Figure 3C4), and TXN-fed mice (Figure 3C5) but was not correlated with energy expenditure in HFD mice (Figure 2C2).
evidence: This claim is supported by linear regression analysis of energy expenditure and caloric intake data.

claim: ANCOVA revealed that LXN, HXN, or TXN supplementation did not change the positive relationship between energy expenditure and body mass.
source: ANCOVA revealed that LXN, HXN, or TXN supplementation did not change the positive relationship between energy expenditure and body mass (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by ANCOVA statistical analysis of energy expenditure data.

claim: TXN treatment restored the negative correlation between caloric intake and plasma TAG.
source: TXN treatment restored the negative correlation between caloric intake and plasma TAG (Spearman r = −0.65, p=0.04; Figure 3—figure supplement 2 A5).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of plasma TAG and caloric intake data.

claim: Fecal TAG levels did not differ among all groups.
source: We collected fecal pellets over a 3 day period and measured fecal TAG at the end of the study as an indicator of fecal energy excretion. Fecal TAG levels did not differ among all groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by fecal TAG measurements showing no significant differences.

claim: The attenuated body weight gain and hepatic steatosis in TXN- and HXN-treated mice was not related to increased fecal TAG excretion.
source: No relationship was observed between caloric intake and fecal TAG among or within groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 2 B1–5), suggesting that the attenuated BW gain and hepatic steatosis in TXN- and HXN-treated mice was not related to increased fecal TAG excretion.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from fecal TAG measurements showing no correlation with caloric intake.

claim: Directed ambulatory locomotion was lower in HFD- than LFD-fed mice.
source: In contrast to energy expenditure (Figure 3C), directed ambulatory locomotion was lower in HFD- than LFD-fed mice (Figure 4A), while fine movement level (Figure 4B) and feeding frequency (Figure 4C) were not changed.
evidence: This claim is supported by activity measurements from metabolic cages.

claim: TXN-treated mice exhibited higher directed ambulatory locomotion and fine movement levels than HFD mice.
source: TXN-treated mice exhibited higher directed ambulatory locomotion and fine movement levels than HFD mice (Figure 4A,B), whereas feeding frequency was unchanged (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by activity measurements from metabolic cages with statistical significance.

claim: XN-treated HFD mice showed higher directed ambulatory locomotion activity and feeding frequency than HFD mice.
source: XN-treated HFD mice showed higher directed ambulatory locomotion activity and feeding frequency than HFD mice (Figure 4A,C), whereas fine movement activity levels were not affected (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by activity measurements from metabolic cages.

claim: In HFD-fed and LXN-treated mice, directed ambulatory locomotion levels were positively correlated with food frequency but negatively correlated with energy expenditure.
source: In HFD-fed and LXN-treated mice, directed ambulatory locomotion levels were positively correlated with food frequency (Figure 4C2-3) but negatively correlated with energy expenditure (Figure 4A2-3), suggesting that food-driven activity may account for a major part of total directed ambulatory motion and that these mice spent the majority of their time and energy moving around for food consumption.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of activity and energy expenditure data.

claim: Diet-induced lipid accumulation differed by adipose site.
source: To assess the effect of XN and TXN on lipid accumulation, fat pads from three distinct sites –subcutaneous (sWAT), epididymal (eWAT), and mesenteric (mWAT) adipose tissue – were carefully removed and weighed during necropsy. Diet-induced lipid accumulation differed by adipose site.
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements of different adipose tissue depots.

claim: The HFD-induced increase in mWAT fat mass was much greater than the increase in sWAT fat mass (3-fold vs. 2.5-fold increase, respectively), with the smallest increase (15%) observed in eWAT fat mass.
source: Compared to the LFD, the HFD-induced increase in mWAT fat mass was much greater than the increase in sWAT fat mass (3-fold vs. 2.5-fold increase, respectively), with the smallest increase (15%) observed in eWAT fat mass (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements of adipose tissue depot masses.

claim: Supplementation with HXN and TXN decreased sWAT and mWAT fat mass.
source: Supplementation with HXN (p<0.05), and even more so TXN (p<0.0001), decreased sWAT and mWAT fat mass.
evidence: This claim is supported by adipose tissue mass measurements with statistical significance.

claim: Caloric intake across diets was positively correlated with sWAT and mWAT fat mass, but no relationship was observed within XN- or TXN-treated groups.
source: Caloric intake across diets was positively correlated with sWAT (r = +0.47; p=0.0002; Figure 5A) and mWAT fat mass (r = +0.39; p=0.002; Figure 5C), but no relationship was observed within XN- or TXN-treated groups (Figure 5A3–5, C3–5), indicating lipid accumulation in sWAT and mWAT fat depots was primarily linked to diet rather than the amount of food consumed.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of adipose tissue mass and caloric intake data.

claim: Mice on a LFD diet possessed hepatic lipid vacuoles and resembled livers of LDLR−/− mice on a similar synthetic diet.
source: Mice on a LFD diet possessed hepatic lipid vacuoles and resembled livers of low-density lipoprotein receptor knock-out (LDLR−/-−) mice on a similar synthetic diet (Lytle and Jump, 2016); however, their liver to BW ratio of about 4% was in a normal healthy range (Lytle et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological observations and citation to published comparisons.

claim: HFD-fed mice had many smaller lipid vacuoles.
source: HFD-fed mice had many smaller lipid vacuoles (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological images shown in Figure 6A.

claim: XN supplementation decreased the number and size of intrahepatic lipid vacuoles in HFD mice in a dose-dependent manner.
source: XN supplementation decreased the number and size of intrahepatic lipid vacuoles in HFD mice in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Supplementation with TXN almost completely prevented hepatic lipid vacuole accumulation in HFD mice, resulting in less lipid accumulation than in LFD mice.
source: Supplementation with TXN almost completely prevented hepatic lipid vacuole accumulation in HFD mice, resulting in less lipid accumulation than in LFD mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: No discernable fibrosis was detected in liver sections using Sirius red staining in any of the mice.
source: We did not detect discernable fibrosis in liver sections using Sirius red staining in any of the mice (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological staining results.

claim: A liver to body weight ratio above 4% indicates NAFLD.
source: The liver to BW ratio is an indicator of NAFLD with a ratio above 4% indicating NAFLD (Lytle et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published diagnostic criteria.

claim: The majority of mice (10 of 12) on a HFD diet had a liver to BW ratio above 4.5%.
source: The majority of mice (10 of 12) on a HFD diet had a liver to BW ratio above 4.5%, whereas all LFD mice had a liver to BW ratio between 3.8% and 4.3% (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by liver to body weight ratio measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Supplementation with HXN decreased the number of mice with a liver to BW ratio above 4% to 4 of 12 mice.
source: Supplementation with HXN decreased the number of mice with a liver to BW ratio above 4% to 4 of 12 mice and all TXN-supplemented mice had a liver to BW ratio below 3.6% except for one, which had a liver to BW ratio of 4% (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by liver to body weight ratio measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: All TXN-supplemented mice had a liver to BW ratio below 3.6% except for one, which had a liver to BW ratio of 4%.
source: Supplementation with HXN decreased the number of mice with a liver to BW ratio above 4% to 4 of 12 mice and all TXN-supplemented mice had a liver to BW ratio below 3.6% except for one, which had a liver to BW ratio of 4% (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by liver to body weight ratio measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Hepatic lipid extracts from TXN-supplemented HFD mice and LFD-fed mice had lower liver triglyceride concentrations than from mice fed with HFD, LXN, or HXN.
source: Hepatic lipid extracts from TXN-supplemented HFD mice and LFD-fed mice had lower liver triglyceride concentrations than from mice fed with HFD, LXN, or HXN (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by hepatic triglyceride measurements shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The histological lower cutoff for NAFLD is over 5% of liver area occupied by lipids.
source: Another indicator of NAFLD is the liver area occupied by lipids; the histological lower cutoff for NAFLD is over 5% of liver area (Brunt, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published diagnostic criteria.

claim: All control HFD mice had NAFLD and 10 of 12 LFD mice had NAFLD using the 5% liver area cutoff.
source: Using this cutoff, all control HFD mice had NAFLD and 10 of 12 LFD mice had NAFLD (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by hepatic lipid area measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both HXN and TXN supplementation decreased liver lipid accumulation on a HFD by twofold.
source: Both HXN and TXN supplementation decreased liver lipid accumulation on a HFD by twofold (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by hepatic lipid area measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: TXN treatment significantly downregulated genes involved in biological processes including xenobiotic catabolism, FA metabolism, glucose metabolism, and regulation of lipid metabolism.
source: GO enrichment analysis indicated that TXN treatment significantly downregulated genes involved in biological processes including xenobiotic catabolism, FA metabolism, glucose metabolism, and regulation of lipid metabolism (Figure 8, top panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 8.

claim: TXN upregulated expression of genes in six pathways including complement and coagulation cascades, prion diseases, steroid hormone biosynthesis, arachidonic acid metabolism, retinol metabolism, and linoleic acid metabolism.
source: Furthermore, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis demonstrated that TXN upregulated expression of genes in six pathways including complement and coagulation cascades, prion diseases, steroid hormone biosynthesis, arachidonic acid metabolism, retinol metabolism, and linoleic acid metabolism (Figure 8, bottom right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by KEGG pathway analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Expression of genes in 25 KEGG pathways were significantly downregulated by TXN treatment compared to HFD.
source: On the other hand, expression of genes in 25 KEGG pathways were significantly downregulated by TXN treatment compared to HFD (Figure 8, bottom left panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by KEGG pathway analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The top 10 significantly enriched KEGG pathways downregulated by TXN included the biosynthesis of unsaturated FAs, glutathione metabolism, amino sugar and nucleotide sugar metabolism, glycolysis and gluconeogenesis, pentose phosphate pathway, fluid shear stress and atherosclerosis, chemical carcinogenesis, drug metabolism, FA elongation, and the PPAR signaling pathway.
source: The top 10 significantly enriched KEGG pathways based on statistical significance and combined score ranking included the biosynthesis of unsaturated FAs, glutathione metabolism, amino sugar and nucleotide sugar metabolism, glycolysis and gluconeogenesis, pentose phosphate pathway, fluid shear stress and atherosclerosis, chemical carcinogenesis, drug metabolism, FA elongation, and the PPAR signaling pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: TXN treatment resulted in a fourfold decrease in Timp2 and Col1a1, both factors that promote hepatic fibrosis.
source: In response to TXN treatment, we noted a fourfold decrease in Timp2 and Col1a1 both factors that promote hepatic fibrosis (Table 2) Nie et al., 2004; Chakraborty et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Table 2 and citation to published research on fibrosis markers.

claim: No changes in expression for Tgfb1 or Pdgf were observed with TXN treatment.
source: We also did not observe changes in expression for transforming growth factor β1 (Tgfb1) or platelet-derived growth factor (Pdgf), key factors in driving hepatic stellate cell activation following hepatocellular injury (data not shown) (Dooley et al., 2001; Tsuchida and Friedman, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis and citation to published research on stellate cell activation.

claim: No increased expression of genes involved in inflammation was observed with 16 weeks of HFD feeding.
source: Finally, we did not observe increased expression of genes involved in inflammation with 16 weeks of HFD feeding, but did observe a significant decrease in Ccr2 and Fgf21 expression with TXN treatment (Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Table 3.

claim: A significant decrease in Ccr2 and Fgf21 expression was observed with TXN treatment.
source: Finally, we did not observe increased expression of genes involved in inflammation with 16 weeks of HFD feeding, but did observe a significant decrease in Ccr2 and Fgf21 expression with TXN treatment (Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Table 3.

claim: Support vector machine identified 13 genes that can distinguish TXN-treated mice from HFD-fed control mice.
source: We implemented support vector machine (SVM) to identify a set of signature genes that can distinguish TXN-treated mice from HFD-fed control mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by machine learning analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Eight of 13 genes identified by SVM showed significant, differential expression between TXN and HFD diet samples.
source: Genes identified classified HFD- and TXN-fed mice into two distinct groups (Figure 9, right panel). Eight of 13 genes showed significant, differential expression between TXN and HFD diet samples (Table 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by SVM analysis and differential expression analysis shown in Figure 9 and Table 5.

claim: Three of the eight significantly regulated genes identified by SVM – Ucp2, Cidec, and Mogat1 – are involved in lipid metabolism and are known target genes of PPARγ.
source: Consistent with the GO analysis, three of the eight genes – uncoupling protein 2 (Ucp2), cell death-inducing DFFA-like effector c (Cidec), and monoacylglycerol O-acyltransferase 1 (Mogat1) – are involved in lipid metabolism and are known target genes of PPARγ (Medvedev et al., 2001; Kim et al., 2008; Matsusue et al., 2008); (Bugge et al., 2010; Karbowska and Kochan, 2012; Wolf Greenstein et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene function analysis and citations to published research on PPARγ target genes.

claim: TXN-treated mice had significantly lower expression of Pparg2 and major PPARγ target genes Cidec, Mogat1, and Plin4 as confirmed by RT-qPCR.
source: We then confirmed expression of these genes using RT-qPCR. Consistent with RNA-seq results, TXN-treated mice had significantly lower expression of Pparg2 and major PPARγ target genes Cidec, Mogat1, and Plin4 (Dalen et al., 2004; Fang et al., 2016; Figure 10, top panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR validation of RNA-seq results shown in Figure 10.

claim: Significantly strong positive correlations were observed between the expression of Cidec, Mogat1, and Plin4.
source: Moreover, we observed significantly strong positive correlations between the expression of these three genes (Figure 10, bottom panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of gene expression data shown in Figure 10.

claim: TXN treatment inhibits the PPARγ pathway, a key pathway involved in hepatic lipid metabolism.
source: The above results suggest TXN treatment inhibits the PPARγ pathway – a key pathway involved in hepatic lipid metabolism.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from gene expression data showing downregulation of PPARγ target genes.

claim: XN and TXN were only significantly cytotoxic for 3T3-L1 cells at a dose of 50 µM.
source: XN and TXN were only significantly cytotoxic for 3T3-L1 cells at a dose of 50 µM (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by MTT cell viability assay results.

claim: Cell viability was greater than 90% at low (5 µM), medium (10 µM), and high (25 µM) concentrations of XN and TXN.
source: While it is difficult to translate in vivo doses to in vitro doses, based on previous in vitro studies (Yang et al., 2007; Samuels et al., 2018) and our current cell viability data, we selected low (5 µM), medium (10 µM), and high (25 µM) concentrations of XN and TXN for the subsequent experiments where cell viability was greater than 90% (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by MTT cell viability assay results and citation to previous studies.

claim: Addition of dexamethasone, IBMX, and insulin strongly induced intracellular lipid accumulation in 3T3-L1 cells.
source: Murine preadipocyte 3T3-L1 differentiation and adipogenesis was induced by the addition of dexamethasone, 3-isobutyl-1-methylxanthine (IBMX), and insulin, which strongly induced intracellular lipid accumulation (Figure 11A2-3).
evidence: This claim is supported by Oil Red O staining results shown in Figure 11.

claim: Addition of XN significantly attenuated intracellular lipid levels in 3T3-L1 cells in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Addition of XN significantly attenuated intracellular lipid levels in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 11B1-3).
evidence: This claim is supported by Oil Red O staining results shown in Figure 11.

claim: TXN strongly inhibited intracellular lipid accumulation in 3T3-L1 cells.
source: Like XN, TXN also strongly inhibit intracellular lipid accumulation (Figure 11C1-3).
evidence: This claim is supported by Oil Red O staining results shown in Figure 11.

claim: Rosiglitazone is a known potent PPARγ agonist used as an insulin-sensitizing agent.
source: RGZ is a known potent PPARγ agonist used as an insulin-sensitizing agent.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about rosiglitazone's pharmacological properties.

claim: RGZ strongly induced 3T3-L1 cell differentiation.
source: RGZ strongly induced the differentiation (Figure 12A1), and GW 9662, a potent PPARγ antagonist, inhibited the RGZ-induced differentiation (Figure 12A2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Oil Red O staining results shown in Figure 12.

claim: GW 9662, a potent PPARγ antagonist, inhibited RGZ-induced 3T3-L1 cell differentiation.
source: RGZ strongly induced the differentiation (Figure 12A1), and GW 9662, a potent PPARγ antagonist, inhibited the RGZ-induced differentiation (Figure 12A2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Oil Red O staining results shown in Figure 12.

claim: Both XN and TXN suppressed RGZ-induced 3T3-L1 differentiation in a dose-dependent manner.
source: We also observed that both XN (Figure 12B1-3) and TXN (Figure 11C1-3) suppressed RGZ-induced differentiation in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by Oil Red O staining results shown in Figure 12.

claim: At 25 µM concentration, RGZ-induced differentiation was largely blocked by XN and TXN.
source: At 25 µM concentration, the RGZ-induced differentiation was largely blocked (Figure 12B3,C3), suggesting that XN and TXN may interfere or even compete with binding of RGZ to the PPARγ receptor.
evidence: This claim is supported by Oil Red O staining results shown in Figure 12 and suggests competitive binding.

claim: The expression of Pparg and its target genes at 7 days post-treatment were significantly downregulated by XN and TXN treatments.
source: To elucidate the effect of XN and TXN on PPARγ action at the transcriptional level, we measured the expression of several known PPARγ target genes using RT-qPCR on samples 7 days post 25 µM XN or TXN treatment. Consistent with the decrease of intracellular lipid content in Figures 11 and 12, the expression of Pparg and its target genes at 7 days post-treatment were significantly downregulated by XN and TXN treatments (Table 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR gene expression data shown in Table 6.

claim: Cells treated with 25 µM XN or TXN significantly reversed the RGZ-induced upregulation of Cd36, Fabp4, Mogat1, Cidec, Plin4, and Fgf21.
source: Cells treated with either 25 µM XN or TXN significantly reversed the RGZ-induced upregulation of Cd36 (p<0.001, p<0.001), Fabp4 (p<0.001, p<0.001), Mogat1 (p<0.001, p<0.01), Cidec (p<0.001, p<0.001), Plin4 (p<0.001, p<0.001), and Fgf21 (p<0.01, p<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR gene expression data with statistical significance.

claim: XN and TXN antagonize PPARγ at the transcriptional level to block 3T3-L1 differentiation.
source: Taken together, these data above suggest that XN and TXN antagonize PPARγ at the transcriptional level to block 3T3-L1 differentiation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from gene expression and differentiation data.

claim: Both XN and TXN displaced a labeled pan-PPARγ ligand in a dose-dependent manner with IC50 values of 1.97 µM and 1.38 µM, respectively.
source: Both XN and TXN displaced a labeled pan-PPARγ ligand (Fluormone Pan-PPAR Green) in a dose-dependent manner with IC50 values of 1.97 µM (Figure 13B) and 1.38 µM (Figure 13C), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by TR-FRET competitive binding assay data shown in Figure 13.

claim: Oleic acid had an IC50 value of 16.6 µM in the PPARγ competitive binding assay.
source: Oleic acid, the most abundant FA ligand in the HFD diet (Table 8), had an IC50 value of 16.6 µM.
evidence: This claim is supported by TR-FRET competitive binding assay data.

claim: XN and TXN had similar IC50 values as the PPARγ ligand PGZ and arachidonic acid.
source: XN and TXN had similar IC50 values as the PPARγ ligand PGZ, a drug used to improve glucose homeostasis and type 2 diabetes, and a natural ligand, arachidonic acid (Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of IC50 values and citation to published data.

claim: The best docked position of TXN occupies the binding site of PPARγ, exhibiting many non-bonded interactions involving side chain atoms in Leu255, Phe264, Gly284, Cys 285, Arg288, Val339, Ile 341, Met348, and Met364.
source: The best docked position of TXN occupies the binding site of PPARγ, exhibiting many non-bonded interactions involving side chain atoms in Leu255, Phe264, Gly284, Cys 285, Arg288, Val339, Ile 341, Met348, and Met364 (Figure 13D).
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular docking simulation results shown in Figure 13D.

claim: The side chains of His266, Arg280, and Ser342 and the main chain carbonyl oxygen atom of Ile281 are well positioned to make electrostatic/hydrogen bonds with the hydroxyl protons and oxygen atoms of the bound TXN molecule.
source: The side chains of His266, Arg280, and Ser342 and the main chain carbonyl oxygen atom of Ile281 are well positioned to make electrostatic/hydrogen bonds with the hydroxyl protons and oxygen atoms of the bound TXN molecule.
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular docking simulation analysis.

claim: Many of the same hydrophobic interactions were observed in the simulated PPARγ-XN and PPARγ-oleic acid complexes.
source: We observed many of the same hydrophobic interactions in the simulated PPARγ-XN (Figure 13E) and PPARγ-oleic acid complexes, and potential electrostatic interactions between His266 and Glu343, or with Arg280 and XN or oleic acid, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular docking simulation results shown in Figure 13E.

claim: The relative binding affinities, ranked in decreasing value of their negative binding energies were, in order, TXN, XN, and oleic acid, consistent with the TR-FRET binding results.
source: The relative binding affinities, ranked in decreasing value of their negative binding energies were, in order, TXN, XN, and oleic acid, consistent with the TR-FRET binding results.
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular docking binding energy calculations that are consistent with experimental binding data.

claim: Three studies propose that XN improves diet-induced hepatic steatosis by suppressing SREBP1c mRNA expression and SREBP activation.
source: Three studies propose that XN improves diet-induced hepatic steatosis by suppressing SREBP1c mRNA expression and SREBP activation (Yui et al., 2014; Miyata et al., 2015; Takahashi and Osada, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published mechanistic studies.

claim: A decrease in hepatic SREPB1c expression was observed with TXN treatment.
source: We also observed a decrease in hepatic SREPB1c expression with TXN treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data from the current study.

claim: Proposed mechanisms for XN's effects include inhibiting pro-inflammatory gene expression, inducing AMPK activation in the liver and skeletal muscle, and enhancing FA oxidation.
source: Others propose mechanisms include inhibiting pro-inflammatory gene expression (Dorn et al., 2010; Mahli et al., 2019), inducing AMPK activation in the liver and skeletal muscle (Costa et al., 2017), and enhancing FA oxidation (Kirkwood et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published mechanistic studies.

claim: Changes in microbiota composition and bile acid metabolism may explain the reduction in weight observed by XN and TXN treatment.
source: We hypothesize that changes in microbiota composition and bile acid metabolism, which can affect nutrient and energy harvesting, may explain the reduction in weight (Wahlström et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2020) observed by treatment, but requires testing in future work.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on hypothesis with citation to supporting literature.

claim: Four pathways generally maintain hepatic lipid homeostasis: uptake of circulating lipids, de novo lipogenesis, FA oxidation, and lipid export in VLDL.
source: Four pathways generally maintain hepatic lipid homeostasis: uptake of circulating lipids, de novo lipogenesis (DNL), FA oxidation (FAO), and lipid export in very low-density lipoproteins (VLDL).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of hepatic lipid metabolism.

claim: These pathways are under tight regulation by hormones, nuclear receptors, and other transcription factors.
source: These pathways are under tight regulation by hormones, nuclear receptors, and other transcription factors (Bechmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge with citation to a review article.

claim: Long-term dysregulation of one and/or multiple hepatic lipid metabolism processes can lead to the development of NAFLD, obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other metabolic disorders.
source: Long-term dysregulation of one and/or multiple processes can lead to the development of NAFLD, obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other metabolic disorders.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of metabolic disease pathogenesis.

claim: No change in transcript levels for genes in pathways regulated by PPARα, namely lipid oxidation, was observed with TXN treatment.
source: We then examined transcript levels for genes in pathways regulated by PPARα, namely lipid oxidation. We observed no change with TXN treatment (Table 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: Most of the gene expression changes with TXN treatment were for genes encoding proteins involved in the lipid storage pathway and regulated by PPARγ.
source: Consistent with the GO enrichment analysis, most of the changes were for genes encoding proteins involved in the lipid storage pathway (Table 4) and regulated by PPARγ.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Table 4 and is consistent with GO analysis.

claim: PPARγ belongs to a super-family of nuclear receptors and its activity requires ligand binding.
source: PPARγ belongs to a super-family of nuclear receptors and just like other members, its activity requires ligand binding.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of nuclear receptor biology.

claim: PPARγ is highly expressed in white and brown adipose tissue, and to a lesser extent in the liver, kidney, and heart.
source: PPARγ is highly expressed in white and brown adipose tissue, and to a lesser extent in the liver, kidney, and heart (Zhu et al., 1993; Lee and Ge, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published expression studies.

claim: PPARγ has been a pharmacological target for drug development in combating metabolic diseases such as insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes.
source: Because of its essential role in regulating adipogenesis and higher expression in the WAT, PPARγ has been a pharmacological target for drug development (Lehmann et al., 1995; Lefterova et al., 2014) in combating metabolic diseases such as insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published drug development literature.

claim: Thiazolidinediones (TZDs), which include RGZ and PGZ, are the most widely investigated PPARγ agonists due to their strong insulin-sensitizing ability.
source: Thiazolidinediones (TZDs), which include RGZ and PGZ, are the most widely investigated PPARγ agonists due to their strong insulin-sensitizing ability (Henney, 2000; Soccio et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published pharmacological studies.

claim: The main action of TZDs occurs in adipocytes.
source: Studies show that the main action of TZDs occurs in adipocytes (Chao et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published mechanistic studies.

claim: Multiple clinical trials using TZDs have observed significant improvement in hepatic steatosis and inflammation.
source: Multiple clinical trials using TZDs have observed significant improvement in hepatic steatosis and inflammation (Ratziu et al., 2008; Ratziu et al., 2010; Sanyal et al., 2010), suggesting additional actions of TZDs in non-adipocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published clinical trial results.

claim: PGZ is more effective in treating fatty liver disease than RGZ, the more potent PPARγ agonist.
source: Interestingly, PGZ is more effective in treating fatty liver disease than RGZ, the more potent PPARγ agonist (Promrat et al., 2004; Ratziu et al., 2008; Ratziu et al., 2010), suggesting that moderate binding is more effective.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published clinical studies and suggests an inference about binding affinity.

claim: Side effects of TZDs include weight gain, bone loss, edema, and increased risk of cardiovascular complications.
source: Unfortunate side effects of TZDs are weight gain (Fonseca, 2003), bone loss (Schwartz and Sellmeyer, 2007; Schwartz, 2008), edema, and increased risk of cardiovascular complications (Nesto et al., 2004; Yang and Soodvilai, 2008; Bełtowski et al., 2013), due to over-activation of PPARγ.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published clinical and safety studies.

claim: The potential of reducing body weight and improving insulin sensitivity suggests a possible clinical role of PPARγ antagonists in treating obesity and type 2 diabetes.
source: The potential of reducing BW and improving insulin sensitivity suggests a possible clinical role of PPARγ antagonists in treating obesity and type 2 diabetes (Yamauchi et al., 2001; Rieusset et al., 2002; Nakano et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is speculative about clinical applications and supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Natural compounds that inhibit PPARγ with moderate binding affinity include resveratrol, 7-chloroarctinone-b, tanshinone IIA, astaxanthin, protopanaxatriol, foenumoside B, and betulinic acid.
source: Compared to agonists, researchers have identified only a few natural compounds that inhibit PPARγ, all of which have a moderate binding affinity for PPARγ receptor and can inhibit adipogenesis, obesity, and/or hepatic steatosis. These include resveratrol (Calleri et al., 2014), 7-chloroarctinone-b isolated from the roots of Rhaponticum uniflorum (Li et al., 2009), tanshinone IIA from the roots of Salvia miltiorrhiza (danshen) (Gong et al., 2009), astaxanthin from red-colored aquatic organisms (Jia et al., 2012), protopanaxatriol extracted from Panax ginseng roots (Zhang et al., 2014), foenumoside B from the herbal plant Lysimachia foenum-graecum (Kwak et al., 2016), and betulinic acid, a pentacyclic triterpene found in the bark of several plants (Brusotti et al., 2017; Ammazzalorso and Amoroso, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies on natural PPARγ antagonists.

claim: XN and TXN accumulate primarily in the liver with significantly lower levels in the muscle.
source: In our previous study, we demonstrated that XN and TXN accumulates primarily in the liver with significantly lower levels in the muscle (Miranda et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous pharmacokinetic study.

claim: XN and TXN could not be detected in the WAT of mice.
source: We could not detect XN or TXN in the WAT of these mice (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue distribution measurements.

claim: The levels of XN and TXN in the liver and the absence of both compounds in the WAT suggest that these compounds antagonize PPARγ in the liver and not in the WAT.
source: The levels of XN and TXN in the liver (TXN > HXN > LXN) and the absence of both compounds in the WAT suggest that these compounds antagonize PPARγ in the liver and not in the WAT, therefore, minimizing the side effect of weight gain observed with TZDs that are PPARγ agonists.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from tissue distribution data.

claim: During long-term HFD feeding, PPARγ and its target genes are upregulated to compensate for the lipid overflow in the liver.
source: During a long-term HFD feeding, PPARγ and its target genes are upregulated to compensate for the lipid overflow in the liver.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from gene expression patterns observed in the study.

claim: Genes associated with lipid uptake and trafficking (Lpl, Cd36, Fabp4), TAG synthesis (Fasn, Scd1, Mogat1), and formation of lipid droplets for storage (Cidec/Fsp27, Plin4) are upregulated during long-term HFD feeding.
source: Namely, genes associated with lipid uptake and trafficking (Lpl, Cd36, Fabp4), TAG synthesis (Fasn, Scd1, Mogat1), and formation of lipid droplets for storage (Cidec/Fsp27, Plin4) (Supplement_File_B).
evidence: This claim is based on gene expression data analysis.

claim: Excessive lipid accumulation in the liver leads to hepatic steatosis.
source: The result is excessive lipid accumulation in the liver, leading to hepatic steatosis.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of NAFLD pathogenesis.

claim: PPARγ overexpression in hepatocytes in ob/ob mice resulted in excessive lipid accumulation.
source: This was observed with PPARγ overexpression in hepatocytes in ob/ob mice (Rahimian et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published genetic studies.

claim: TXN antagonizes PPARγ action in the liver potentially by physically interacting with PPARγ receptors and reduces PPARγ transcriptional activity and expression of target genes.
source: We propose that TXN added to a HFD antagonizes PPARγ action in the liver potentially by physically interacting with PPARγ receptors as indicated in the molecular docking studies (Figure 13DE) and, therefore, reduces PPARγ transcriptional activity and expression of the aforementioned target genes.
evidence: This claim is a proposed mechanism based on inference from multiple experimental results including docking studies.

claim: Hepatocyte- and macrophage-specific PPARγ deficiency protects Lep<ob/ob> mice from hepatic steatosis.
source: Several in vivo studies support our findings. Hepatocyte- and macrophage-specific PPARγ deficiency protects Lep < ob/ob> mice from hepatic steatosis (Matsusue et al., 2003; Morán-Salvador et al., 2011); knockdown of Mogat1 in the liver significantly attenuates hepatic steatosis after 12 weeks HFD feeding (Lee et al., 2012); and restoration of Cidec/Fsp27 in Lep < ob/ob> liver-specific Pparg knockout mice promotes hepatic steatosis (Matsusue et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published genetic studies in mice.

claim: Knockdown of Mogat1 in the liver significantly attenuates hepatic steatosis after 12 weeks HFD feeding.
source: Several in vivo studies support our findings. Hepatocyte- and macrophage-specific PPARγ deficiency protects Lep < ob/ob> mice from hepatic steatosis (Matsusue et al., 2003; Morán-Salvador et al., 2011); knockdown of Mogat1 in the liver significantly attenuates hepatic steatosis after 12 weeks HFD feeding (Lee et al., 2012); and restoration of Cidec/Fsp27 in Lep < ob/ob> liver-specific Pparg knockout mice promotes hepatic steatosis (Matsusue et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published genetic studies.

claim: Restoration of Cidec/Fsp27 in Lep<ob/ob> liver-specific Pparg knockout mice promotes hepatic steatosis.
source: Several in vivo studies support our findings. Hepatocyte- and macrophage-specific PPARγ deficiency protects Lep < ob/ob> mice from hepatic steatosis (Matsusue et al., 2003; Morán-Salvador et al., 2011); knockdown of Mogat1 in the liver significantly attenuates hepatic steatosis after 12 weeks HFD feeding (Lee et al., 2012); and restoration of Cidec/Fsp27 in Lep < ob/ob> liver-specific Pparg knockout mice promotes hepatic steatosis (Matsusue et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published genetic studies.

claim: Ablation of Pparg in murine myeloid cells increased insulin resistance.
source: Ablation of Pparg in murine myeloid cells increased insulin resistance (Souza et al., 2020) and ablation in macrophages and hepatic stellate cells, but not hepatocytes increased inflammation (Morán-Salvador et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published genetic studies.

claim: Ablation of Pparg in macrophages and hepatic stellate cells, but not hepatocytes, increased inflammation.
source: Ablation of Pparg in murine myeloid cells increased insulin resistance (Souza et al., 2020) and ablation in macrophages and hepatic stellate cells, but not hepatocytes increased inflammation (Morán-Salvador et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published genetic studies.

claim: TXN did not promote hepatic inflammation.
source: Nevertheless, we did not observe either of these conditions in our study. In contrast, TXN did not promote hepatic inflammation (Table 2) but improved glucose clearance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Table 2.

claim: Complete absence of PPARγ is quite different from modulating its activity through agonists and antagonists.
source: We postulate complete the absence of PPARγ is quite different from modulating its activity through agonists and antagonists, and this may explain the differences noted in some of these cell-specific knockout studies and our findings.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning to explain differences between genetic knockout studies and pharmacological modulation.

claim: Gut microbiota dysbiosis has been observed in obesity and type 2 diabetes, which are diseases strongly associated with NAFLD.
source: Gut microbiota dysbiosis has been observed in obesity and type 2 diabetes, which are diseases strongly associated with NAFLD.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of the relationship between microbiota and metabolic disease.

claim: Mouse studies and fecal transplantation experiments have demonstrated a causal role of gut microbiota in the development of NAFLD.
source: Mouse studies and fecal transplantation experiments have demonstrated a causal role of gut microbiota in the development of NAFLD (Henao-Mejia et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published experimental studies.

claim: Both XN and TXN drastically changed gut microbiota composition in C57Bl6/J male mice, accompanied with a significant change in the fecal bile acid composition.
source: We previously reported that both XN and TXN drastically changed gut microbiota composition in C57Bl6/J male mice, accompanied with a significant change in the fecal bile acid composition (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous published work.

claim: Administration of XN and TXN decreased intestinal microbiota diversity and abundance, altered bile acid metabolism, and reduced inflammation.
source: Specifically, administration of XN and TXN decreased intestinal microbiota diversity and abundance, altered bile acid metabolism, and reduced inflammation.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' previous published work.

claim: Changes in the gut microbiota and bile acid metabolism may also explain, in part, the improvements in MetS and NAFLD.
source: Changes in the gut microbiota and bile acid metabolism may also explain, in part, the improvements in MetS and NAFLD, but requires investigation in future studies.
evidence: This claim is speculative about mechanisms requiring future investigation.

claim: Feeding XN to Zucker fa/fa rats for 6 weeks significantly lowered body weight gain and plasma glucose levels only in male, but not female rats.
source: Legette et al. reported feeding XN to Zucker fa/fa rats for 6 weeks significantly lowered BW gain and plasma glucose levels only in male, but not female rats (Legette et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published animal studies showing sex differences.

claim: The gender difference in response to XN is not unique as similar findings were observed for other flavonoids.
source: This gender difference in response to XN is not unique as similar findings were observed for other flavonoids (Camper-Kirby et al., 2001; Blair et al., 2002; Guo et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies on other flavonoids.

claim: The expression of numerous major urinary protein (Mup) genes was reduced by a HFD as compared to the LFD.
source: Consistent with a prior study (Zhou et al., 2009), we found the expression of numerous major urinary protein (Mup) genes reduced by a HFD as compared to the LFD; however, the expression of these same genes were induced by TXN administration (Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Table 3 and citation to a previous study.

claim: The expression of Mup genes were induced by TXN administration.
source: Consistent with a prior study (Zhou et al., 2009), we found the expression of numerous major urinary protein (Mup) genes reduced by a HFD as compared to the LFD; however, the expression of these same genes were induced by TXN administration (Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Table 3.

claim: MUPs are unique members of the lipocalin super-family produced by the liver and secreted into urine primarily in males.
source: MUPs are unique members of the lipocalin super-family produced by the liver and secreted into urine primarily in males (Zhou and Rui, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research on MUP biology.

claim: MUPs function in the urine as pheromones in chemical communication and as metabolic signals regulating glucose and lipid metabolism in individual animals.
source: They function in the urine as pheromones in chemical communication and as metabolic signals regulating glucose and lipid metabolism in individual animal (Zhou and Rui, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research on MUP function.

claim: Adult male mice secrete significantly more MUPs than females.
source: Because adult male mice secrete significantly more MUPs than females, this finding may explain why female mice do not respond to XN and TXN like their male counterparts.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of sex differences in MUP secretion and used to infer an explanation for sex differences in response to treatment.

claim: TXN treatment beneficially modulated expression of lipocalin members, Lcn2 and ApoM.
source: TXN treatment also beneficially modulated expression of lipocalin members, Lcn2 and ApoMm (Wang et al., 2007; Milner et al., 2009; Auguet et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data and citations to published research on these lipocalins.

claim: In NAFLD, metabolically active tissues often present a chronic low-grade inflammation characterized by the recruitment of pro-inflammatory cells, cytokines, and acute-phase proteins.
source: To maintain energy homeostasis, proper crosstalk between metabolically active tissues is essential (Stern et al., 2016). In NAFLD (and MetS in general), these tissues often present a chronic low-grade inflammation characterized by the recruitment of pro-inflammatory cells, cytokines, and acute-phase proteins (Lackey and Olefsky, 2016; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research on NAFLD pathophysiology.

claim: Supplementation with TXN decreased chronic inflammation with reduced expression of major pro-inflammatory cytokines Il6 and Tnfα in WAT and to a smaller extent in the liver.
source: Previously we reported that supplementation with TXN decreased chronic inflammation with reduced expression of major pro-inflammatory cytokines Il6 and Tnfα in WAT and to a smaller extent in the liver (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous published work.

claim: A decrease in Ccl2, a chemotactic factor involved in the recruitment of monocytes, and macrophage marker F4/80 in WAT was observed with TXN treatment.
source: We also observed a decrease in Ccl2, a chemotactic factor involved in the recruitment of monocytes, and macrophage marker F4/80 in WAT, suggesting that TXN may protect WAT from macrophage infiltration (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous published work and suggests a protective mechanism.

claim: The dose of TXN given in the diet is very effective in suppressing the development and progression of diet-induced hepatic steatosis in mice.
source: In conclusion, we demonstrated the dose of TXN given in the diet is very effective in suppressing the development and progression of diet-induced hepatic steatosis in mice.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data from the study.

claim: TXN appears more effective in vivo than XN perhaps due to significantly higher levels of TXN in the liver.
source: TXN appears more effective in vivo than XN perhaps due to significantly higher levels of TXN in the liver, but XN can slow progression of the condition at a higher dose.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparative efficacy and pharmacokinetic data.

claim: At the dose used for TXN, no adverse events were observed in prior or current studies.
source: At the dose used for TXN, we have not observed adverse events in our prior or current studies (Miranda et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by safety observations from the current study and citation to previous work.

claim: XN and TXN are effective preventative approaches in rodents.
source: While XN and TXN are effective preventative approaches in rodents, in future studies we are interested in determining if these compounds can treat existing obesity.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data and indicates future research directions.

claim: XN and TXN bind to PPARγ with a similar affinity as the agonist PGZ.
source: We provide evidence that XN and TXN act as novel, natural, and synthetic antagonists of PPARγ that bind with a similar affinity as the agonist PGZ.
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive binding assay data comparing IC50 values.

claim: The findings support further development of XN and TXN as novel, low-cost therapeutic compounds for diet-linked hepatic steatosis with fewer negative side effects than current drugs.
source: Our findings support further development of XN and TXN as novel, low-cost therapeutic compounds for diet-linked hepatic steatosis with fewer negative side effects than current drugs (e.g., reduced adipose tissue expansion).
evidence: This claim is a conclusion and recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: The structures of XN and TXN could serve as scaffolds for the synthesis of more effective compounds to treat NAFLD and other fatty liver diseases.
source: Additionally, the structures of XN and TXN could serve as scaffolds for the synthesis of more effective compounds to treat NAFLD and other fatty liver diseases.
evidence: This claim is speculative about future drug development possibilities.

claim: These findings raise the possibility of testing XN and TXN in combination with other PPARγ ligands in treating obesity and metabolic syndrome.
source: These findings also raise the possibility of testing XN and TXN in combination with other PPARγ ligands in treating obesity and metabolic syndrome.
evidence: This claim is speculative about future research directions.

claim: Further studies are required to clarify possible use of XN and TXN in humans for the prevention and treatment of diet-linked hepatic steatosis.
source: Although these results are encouraging, further studies are required to clarify possible use in humans for the prevention and treatment of diet-linked hepatic steatosis.
evidence: This claim acknowledges the need for future human studies before clinical application.
